0.title: Habakkuk: The Righteous Shall Live by Faith
0.overview:
The message. Habakkuk is the book for anyone who has looked at the world and wanted to argue with God. Violence fills the streets of Judah, the courts are bent, and God seems to do nothing; then God says he is bringing the Babylonians, who are crueller still. Habakkuk takes both troubles straight to God, and God answers, not with a full explanation, but with a promise that every wrong will be judged at his appointed time, and a call to trust him until then: “the righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4). The book opens with a complaint, “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?” (1:2), and closes with a song of joy in God when everything else has gone (3:17–19). It shows how a faith that cannot see becomes a faith that sings.

Background: the prophet. We know almost nothing about Habakkuk beyond his name and his calling, “Habakkuk the prophet” (1:1; 3:1). Unlike most prophets he names no father, no home town and no king. Martin Luther took his unusual name to mean one who embraces, a prophet who holds his people close in a hard time. A later legend, in Bel and the Dragon, an addition to Daniel in the Greek Bible, has an angel carry him to Babylon to feed Daniel in the lions’ den; it has no claim on history.

When and where. Josiah’s reform, from 622 BC, had cleared away the idols and restored the law. After he was killed in battle in 609 BC, his son Jehoiakim (609–598 BC) soon undid it; Jeremiah condemned him as one “who builds his house by unrighteousness” and has eyes only “for shedding innocent blood” (Jeremiah 22:13, 17). That is the violence and the paralysed law of 1:2–4. Meanwhile the Chaldeans, the Babylonians, had destroyed Nineveh, Assyria’s capital, in 612 BC, and in 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar crushed Egypt at Carchemish. God’s word that he was “raising up the Chaldeans” (1:6), a work “you would not believe if told” (1:5), most likely came about that time, about 605 BC; some date it a little earlier, while Babylon’s rise still looked unlikely. Soon Jehoiakim “became his servant for three years” (2 Kings 24:1); Jerusalem was taken in 597 BC and burned in 586 BC (see the kings of Israel and Judah). And Babylon in its turn fell to Cyrus in 539 BC, as the woes of chapter 2 had warned.

The kind of writing. Habakkuk calls his book an “oracle” (1:1), a weighty word from God, but it is built like no other prophetic book. Most prophets speak for God to the people; Habakkuk speaks to God for the people, and writes down both sides of the conversation. Then come five woes (2:6–20), a taunt song the plundered nations sing over their oppressor. Last comes a psalm, with a musical heading, “Selah” three times and a note for the choirmaster (3:1, 19). Its picture of God marching out, the mountains writhing and the sun and moon standing still (3:6–11), is the poetry of the exodus and Sinai: the prophet recalls what God has done in order to trust what he will do. Some scholars think chapter 3 was added later, partly because the commentary on Habakkuk among the Dead Sea Scrolls (see the Essenes) covers only chapters 1–2; but its heading names Habakkuk, and it answers the waiting commanded in 2:3. This commentary reads the book as one.

How the book makes its case. The book moves from why, to wait, to worship. First Habakkuk complains that God ignores the injustice in Judah (1:2–4), and God answers that he is raising up the Chaldeans (1:5–11). That answer is harder than the question, and the prophet comes back with a sharper one: how can God, who is “of purer eyes than to see evil”, stay silent “when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?” (1:13). Then he climbs his watchpost to wait (2:1). God tells him to write the vision plainly, for it has an appointed time: “If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay” (2:3). The proud conqueror is set beside the righteous who live by faith (2:4–5), and five woes fall on plunder, unjust gain, cities built with blood, degrading one’s neighbours and dead idols (2:6–19). In the middle stands the promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory (2:14), and at the end a hush: “let all the earth keep silence before him” (2:20). In chapter 3 the prophet prays, “in wrath remember mercy” (3:2), remembers the exodus, trembles at what is coming, resolves to wait, and rejoices in God though every crop fails. His questions are never fully answered; the questioner is changed.

Faith or faithfulness? The Hebrew word in 2:4 usually means faithfulness, steadiness that can be relied on, as the ESV footnote says, and some therefore think Paul made it say more than it does. The Greek Old Testament even reads “my faithfulness”, meaning God’s. This commentary’s view is that the steadiness in view is the steadiness of trust. The righteous man is set against one whose “soul is puffed up” (2:4) with self-reliance, and he is told to hold on to a promise he cannot yet see (2:2–3). Faith and faithfulness are not rivals: faith leans on God, and faithfulness is that leaning kept up day after day. Neither earns life; both receive it. Paul draws out what is already there in it.

Where it leads: to Christ. Habakkuk leads to Christ by the question it raises and by the promise it gives. Its question is how a holy God can let the wicked swallow up the righteous and still be holy (1:13). At the cross the wicked swallowed up the one truly righteous man, and heaven seemed silent; yet Peter preached that Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and there God showed that he is “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). There God in wrath remembered mercy. The cup in the LORD’s right hand that comes round to the oppressor (2:16) is the cup Jesus prayed would pass from him, and then drank (Matthew 26:39). The promise of 2:4 becomes, in Paul, the heart of the gospel: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, ‘The righteous shall live by faith’” (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Through those words Luther came to peace with God. Hebrews reads the vision that “will surely come” (2:3) as the return of Christ: “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay” (Hebrews 10:37). And when God goes out “for the salvation of your anointed” (3:13), the word is the one from which “Messiah” comes; many Christians rightly hear behind the king of Habakkuk’s day the one Anointed through whom God saves.

For us. Habakkuk gives Christians permission to bring God their real questions, and shows what to do next: wait for his word, be willing to be corrected by it, and live by trusting him when the evidence points the other way. The book does not promise that the fig tree will blossom; it promises God. Believers in Christ can say Habakkuk’s “yet” with more reason than he could, for the God “who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32) will not let them go, and the world filled with his glory will surely come. So when the fields are bare we can still say with the prophet, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation” (3:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — How Long Shall I Cry for Help?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith may bring God its hardest questions, and bring them to his face. Habakkuk is a prophet who speaks to God for the people rather than to the people for God (v. 1). His first words are a complaint: he has cried for help and God has not heard; he is made to watch violence and strife while God seems to look on and do nothing (vv. 2–3). The result is a society where the law has gone numb and justice comes out bent, because the wicked hem in the righteous (v. 4). Scripture keeps this prayer so that we may learn to pray like it.
verseByVerse.theology: God allows his people to bring him their hardest questions, and a prophet's honest protest is part of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This book is a weighty word God gave Habakkuk to see, and it begins not with a message to the people but with a prophet’s prayer.

Habakkuk the prophet. His name appears nowhere else in Scripture (see the introduction), and his book is built differently from the others. Other prophets carry God’s word down to the people; this man carries the people’s questions up, and then writes down what God says back.

The setting. Babylon has not yet arrived, though it is coming (v. 6), and the corruption that the good king Josiah cleared away is back (vv. 2–4). The king was probably Jehoiakim (609–598 BC), of whom Jeremiah said, “Woe to him who builds his house by unrighteousness” (Jeremiah 22:13).

A prayer, not an essay. Habakkuk is not writing an essay about suffering. He is praying, and the prayer is kept in Scripture so that we may pray like it.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk prophesied shortly before Babylon’s invasions of Judah, around 605 BC. The book is a dialogue: the prophet’s complaints and God’s answers.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you "Violence!" and you will not save? Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong? Destruction and violence are before me; strife and contention arise. So the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth. For the wicked surround the righteous; so justice goes forth perverted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Habakkuk complains to God’s face that he neither hears nor acts while violence fills Judah and justice is twisted, and he complains as a believer.

O LORD, how long shall I cry for help. The book’s first words are a complaint. “How long” is the cry the psalms raise in dark times: “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). Even the martyrs in heaven cry “how long” (Revelation 6:10).

You will not hear. Habakkuk says God is not listening, and he says it straight to God. That is the difference between unbelief and honest faith: he does not walk away, but takes his complaint to the only one who can do anything about it.

Why do you idly look at wrong? The sharpest part of the protest. The problem is not that God cannot see, but that he seems to watch and do nothing.

The law is paralyzed. The complaint is about his own country: destruction and violence in the streets, strife and contention everywhere. The courts exist and the statutes are on the books, but nothing happens. The word means grown numb: the law has lost its grip. And when justice does move, it comes out bent, because the wicked hem in the righteous on every side.

God is not offended. Scripture is not embarrassed by this prayer, and God is not offended by his children asking why. But notice what Habakkuk does next: he waits for an answer (2:1).

Where does the outrage come from? Many people now make Habakkuk’s complaint against God: if he is there, why does he let this go on? Scripture lets a prophet ask it first. But the complaint assumes that violence is really wrong, not merely unpleasant, and that a bent court is an outrage, not just an unlucky outcome. Without God it is hard to keep standing on that ground. Richard Dawkins, writing as an atheist in River Out of Eden (1995), said the universe looks exactly as we should expect if at bottom there is “no design, no purpose, no evil and no good, nothing but blind, pitiless indifference.” He was being consistent. But nobody can protest to indifference. Habakkuk could cry “how long” because he knew there was a court of appeal, and a Judge who cared about justice more than he did. The answer would come in a form he could not yet imagine: the Judge himself condemned in the place of the guilty at the cross, so that justice and mercy could both be done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — I Am Raising Up the Chaldeans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is at work when he seems idle, but his work may be harder than our prayers. He tells Judah to look among the nations, for he is doing something they would not believe if told (v. 5): he is raising up the Chaldeans, bitter, swift and answerable only to themselves (vv. 6–7). Their cavalry is faster than leopards and fiercer than wolves at dusk; they gather captives like sand and laugh at kings and fortresses (vv. 8–10). Yet God has already passed his verdict on them: guilty men, whose own might is their god (v. 11). He uses them, but he does not approve of them, and their turn will come.
verseByVerse.theology: God rules the rise of empires, and his answers to prayer are often harder than we expected.

verseByVerse.quote: "Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded. For I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe if told. For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation, who march through the breadth of the earth, to seize dwellings not their own. They are dreaded and fearsome; their justice and dignity go forth from themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers that he is at work after all, but in a way Habakkuk would never have believed: he is raising up the Babylonians, a ruthless nation answerable to no one.

Look among the nations, and see. God has not been idle (v. 3). He is doing “a work in your days”, so astonishing that no one would believe it if simply told.

I am raising up the Chaldeans. The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, the rising superpower, and the answer lands like a blow: God’s response to injustice in Judah is to bring in an army far more violent than anything in Jerusalem. And see who is acting. God does not merely permit Babylon; he raises it up. Jeremiah, preaching at the same time, even calls Nebuchadnezzar “my servant” (Jeremiah 25:9), a tool in God’s hand. God governs nations that do not know him, and uses them without approving of them (v. 11).

Their justice and dignity go forth from themselves. Bitter, hasty and grasping, they make their own rules and answer to nobody. That is the mark of every tyranny, ancient or modern.

A work you would not believe. Paul quoted verse 5 at the close of his synagogue sermon in Pisidian Antioch, warning his hearers not to be scoffers who miss what God is doing (Acts 13:40–41). The unbelievable work in their days was greater than Babylon: God had raised Jesus, and through him “forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you” (Acts 13:38).

Beyond Babylon. If God can raise up an empire, he also rules the governments, employers and illnesses that shape our lives. That truth is terrifying if God is only powerful, and steadying if he is also good.

Textual note. Paul follows the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which has “you scoffers” where the Hebrew has “among the nations”.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quoted v. 5 as a warning in his synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch.

verseByVerse.quote: Their horses are swifter than leopards, more fierce than the evening wolves; their horsemen press proudly on. Their horsemen come from afar; they fly like an eagle swift to devour. They all come for violence, all their faces forward. They gather captives like sand. At kings they scoff, and at rulers they laugh. They laugh at every fortress, for they pile up earth and take it. Then they sweep by like the wind and go on, guilty men, whose own might is their god!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God paints the Babylonian army as a swift, unstoppable predator, and then gives his verdict on it: guilty men whose god is their own strength.

Swifter than leopards. A portrait of a war machine. Their horses are faster than leopards and fiercer than the wolves that hunt at dusk, and their horsemen swoop “like an eagle swift to devour”. Moses had warned that a covenant-breaking Israel would meet such a nation, “swooping down like the eagle” (Deuteronomy 28:49).

They gather captives like sand. Countless people, worth nothing to them. Kings are a joke, and so are fortresses: they pile an earth ramp against the wall and walk in.

Whose own might is their god! God’s own verdict on the army he is sending: “guilty men”. Babylon is not innocent, and its turn will come in chapter 2.

A hard doctrine and a comfort. That God directs even such an army is hard, and comforting: nothing in history is out of control. But God’s answers to our prayers sometimes come in a shape we would never have chosen.

Uncertain wording. The key word in “all their faces forward” occurs only here in the Old Testament. It may mean the eager set of their faces; the KJV took it as “as the east wind”. Either way the army presses on without turning aside.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Why Do You Idly Look?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith argues with God from who God is, and refuses to believe that cruelty has the last word. Habakkuk begins with what he knows: God is everlasting, his Holy One and his Rock, so his people will not die, and the Chaldeans are God’s appointed instrument of correction (v. 12). Then he presses the harder question: how can a God too pure to look on evil stay silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves? (v. 13). The conqueror hauls in nations like fish, worships the net that feeds him, and grows fat on the catch (vv. 14–16). Will it go on forever? (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith argues with God on the basis of who God is, and refuses to accept that cruelty has the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you not from everlasting, O LORD my God, my Holy One? We shall not die. O LORD, you have ordained them as a judgment, and you, O Rock, have established them for reproof. You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? You make mankind like the fish of the sea, like crawling things that have no ruler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Habakkuk steadies himself on who God is, everlasting, holy and his Rock, and then asks his hardest question: how can so pure a God stay silent while the wicked devour people more righteous than themselves?

Are you not from everlasting? He does not start with his objection but with God: “O LORD my God, my Holy One”, “O Rock”. He reasons from God’s character to his confusion, not the other way round.

We shall not die. In the middle stands a statement of faith that carries the whole book. Whatever this invasion means, it cannot mean the end of God’s people, because the everlasting God has bound himself to them.

You have ordained them as a judgment. He accepts the Babylonians as God’s instrument, established “for reproof”, to correct his people. He is not fighting the doctrine of God’s sovereignty; he is struggling with something else.

Of purer eyes than to see evil. Here is the real question of the book, sharper than the first. Habakkuk believes two things that seem impossible together: God is utterly holy, unable to look on wrong and let it be, and God is using a nation far worse than Judah to punish Judah. How can he “remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he”? Put bluntly, the Holy One seems to have taken the bully’s side, and Habakkuk will not pretend otherwise.

Like the fish of the sea. People are treated like fish, or like crawling things with no ruler to protect them. That is what conquest does: it reduces human beings made in God’s image to a catch.

The wicked swallowed up the righteous. Habakkuk’s question has one supreme instance. At the cross the wicked swallowed up the only truly righteous man, and heaven seemed silent. Yet Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). God used guilty hands without excusing them, as he did with Babylon, and out of the worst injustice in history he brought the salvation of the world. That does not answer every why, but it shows that God’s silence is not his absence.

Every believer’s question. Every believer meets this question: not why there is suffering in the abstract, but why those who trample others seem to prosper while those who try to do right are trodden down. Asaph asked it in Psalm 73, and it wore him out “until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end” (Psalm 73:17).

How can a holy God use a worse nation to punish Judah? His holiness is not compromised by using a guilty instrument, because he judges the instrument in turn. The five woes on Babylon follow (2:6–20), as Assyria, “the rod of my anger”, was punished for its arrogance after God had used it (Isaiah 10:5–12). Meanwhile “the righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4), trusting the God whose justice is never late.

Textual note. Ancient Jewish scribal tradition says that “We shall not die” may once have read You do not die, speaking of God. The point stands either way: because the everlasting God cannot die, his people will not perish.

verseByVerse.quote: He brings all of them up with a hook; he drags them out with his net; he gathers them in his dragnet; so he rejoices and is glad. Therefore he sacrifices to his net and makes offerings to his dragnet; for by them he lives in luxury, and his food is rich. Is he then to keep on emptying his net and mercilessly killing nations forever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conqueror hauls in whole nations like fish and then worships the net that feeds him, and Habakkuk asks whether it will go on forever.

He brings all of them up with a hook. The conqueror, the wicked man of verse 13, hauls nations in with hook, net and dragnet, and the catch makes him glad.

He sacrifices to his net. The detail that says everything about him: he worships his own equipment, because by it “he lives in luxury, and his food is rich” (literally, his portion is fat). Babylon’s religion was, in the end, admiration of Babylon’s methods: the army, the siege ramps, the machinery of empire. Assyria had boasted the same way: “By the strength of my hand I have done it” (Isaiah 10:13).

Sacrificing to the net today. A business can worship its own model, a country its army or its economy, a person his own competence and hard work. The test is simple: what do we thank when things go well?

Another net. Jesus also sent fishermen to catch people (Luke 5:10), but for life. The conqueror’s net takes lives to feed himself; Christ gathers people in to feed them, and paid for the catch with his own life.

Is he then to keep on emptying his net? The chapter ends on an unanswered question: will it always be like this, “forever”? In the next chapter Habakkuk climbs his watchpost to wait for God’s reply (2:1), the right instinct when our questions have run out: not to pretend we have answers, but to take our stand and wait for the God who answers.

1.title: O LORD, How Long?
1.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 opens the book, and there is no sermon to the people in it, only a prophet arguing with God. It holds a complaint, God’s startling answer, and a second, sharper complaint that leaves the prophet waiting at his watchpost (2:1).

The message. God hears the cry of his people even when he seems silent, and he is at work in history even when he seems idle; but his work may be harder than anything we would have asked for. Faith may bring him its hardest questions, and it argues from who God is: everlasting, holy, our Rock.

Why it was said. Under Jehoiakim, Judah had thrown off Josiah’s reform: violence filled the streets, the courts no longer worked, and Babylon was rising (see the introduction). The faithful needed to know whether God saw, and what he was doing.

How the chapter makes its case. After the heading (v. 1) comes the first complaint: how long will you not hear, and why do you watch wrong and do nothing? (vv. 2–4). God answers that he is doing a work they would not believe: he is raising up the Chaldeans, swift, fearsome and answerable to no one, guilty men whose own might is their god (vv. 5–11). The prophet answers back, holding on to who God is, “We shall not die” (v. 12), and pressing the harder question: how can the Holy One stay silent while the wicked swallow the righteous? (v. 13). People have become fish in the conqueror’s net, the net has become his god, and will it go on forever? (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The chapter’s question, how a holy God can let the wicked swallow up the righteous (v. 13), has its sharpest instance at the cross, where lawless men killed the one truly righteous man, yet according to “the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). There God judged sin and saved sinners, and showed himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And Habakkuk’s cry that God does not hear is taken up by the Son, who cried “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), and was heard, and raised.

For us. Christians may bring God their honest complaints, and should, but as Habakkuk did: to God’s face, holding on to who he is, and ready to be answered. When God’s ways are darker than our prayers, the cross gives us a place to stand: his silence is not his absence, and no wrong will go unjudged.
1.theology:
God welcomes the honest protest of faith; lament belongs in Scripture and in prayer (vv. 2-4; Ps 13:1; Rev 6:10).

God is at work even when he appears idle, and his work may be beyond what we would believe (v. 5; Acts 13:41).

God raises up and rules nations that do not know him, using them without excusing them (vv. 6, 11; Jer 25:9).

Faith starts from what it knows of God’s character and brings its confusion to him; it does not let confusion lead it to doubt God (v. 12).

The hardest problem is not suffering in general but the prospering of the violent, and Scripture takes the question seriously (v. 13; Ps 73:16-17).

People who succeed by force end by worshipping their own methods (v. 16).

When our questions run out, the right response is to take our stand and wait for God to answer (v. 17; 2:1).
1.examples:
Here is a prophet who takes the people's questions to God instead of God's answers to the people, in a land where the courts are open, the laws are on the books and justice never arrives.

The answer to his prayer is harder than the problem: cavalry faster than leopards and hungrier than wolves at dusk, prisoners counted like grains of sand, and a conqueror burning incense to his own fishing net.

keyVerse.quote: You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?
keyVerse.note: This is the question the whole book wrestles with, and it is sharper than the first complaint because it rests on God’s own holiness. Habakkuk does not doubt that God is pure; that is exactly what makes his silence so hard to bear. God answers it in stages, with the vision and the woes of chapter 2 and the song of chapter 3, and finally at the cross, where the wicked swallowed up the Righteous One and God stayed holy while he saved.

1.reflection:
Habakkuk takes his complaint straight to God (vv. 2–4). What is the difference between complaining to God and complaining about him? Is there something you need to bring to him as honestly as this?

God’s answer was harder than the problem Habakkuk prayed about (vv. 5–11). Have you known God answer a prayer in a way you would never have chosen? What helped you keep trusting him in it?

Before he asks his hardest question, Habakkuk steadies himself on who God is: everlasting, holy, his Rock (v. 12). Which truths about God hold you up when you cannot understand what he is doing?

The conqueror “sacrifices to his net” (v. 16). What do people around us thank when things go well, and what does it look like to thank God instead? How does the cross, where the wicked swallowed up the righteous one, change the way you face the injustice you see now?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word will come at its appointed time, and until it does, the righteous live by trusting him. Habakkuk stations himself like a watchman to wait for God’s answer, ready to be corrected (v. 1). God tells him to write the vision plainly, large enough to read at a glance, for it has an appointed time: if it seems slow, wait for it, because it will surely come (vv. 2–3). Then the heart of the book. The proud man is puffed up and crooked within, drunk on success and as greedy as the grave; but the righteous shall live by his faith (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to the delay of justice is a promise to be trusted, and the righteous live by trusting it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will take my stand at my watchpost and station myself on the tower, and look out to see what he will say to me, and what I will answer concerning my complaint. And the LORD answered me: "Write the vision; make it plain on tablets, so he may run who reads it. For still the vision awaits its appointed time; it hastens to the end—it will not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come; it will not delay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Habakkuk waits for God’s answer, and God tells him to write it down plainly, because it will certainly come at the time he has fixed, however slow it seems.

I will take my stand at my watchpost. Having fired his questions, Habakkuk does what few of us do: he waits for the answer, like a watchman on the city wall scanning the horizon.

What I will answer concerning my complaint. He expects God to speak, and he expects to be corrected: God’s reply may show him that his complaint was wrong. Honest prayer includes the willingness to be answered.

Write the vision; make it plain on tablets. God does answer, and first he says, write it down, plain enough “so he may run who reads it”: legible at a glance, like a notice on a wall, for anyone to take in and carry away. This is one reason we have a Bible: God’s answers are not private impressions but written words, to be read and passed on long after the prophet is dead.

For still the vision awaits its appointed time. Here is God’s answer to the problem of delay. He has a date for it, and the date is fixed; and “it will not lie”: it is not an empty comfort.

If it seems slow, wait for it. The words that have steadied believers ever since. “If it seems slow” is honest: God does not pretend that waiting is easy or that his timing feels quick to us. What looks slow to us is exactly on time from where he stands (2 Peter 3:9).

The coming one will come. Hebrews quotes this verse to a church tempted to give up under pressure, and applies it to the return of Christ: “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay” (Hebrews 10:37). The final answer to every unanswered prayer is Christ himself, and he is coming.

Is this a mandate for church vision statements? No. “The vision” is God’s revealed word of judgment and promise (vv. 3–20), written plainly so that a herald could run with it or a reader take it in at a glance. It is not about a leader’s plans or personal goals.

Uncertain wording. “So he may run who reads it” is compressed in Hebrew. It may mean that a herald who reads it can run to spread the news, or that it can be read easily, even in passing. Both point the same way: God wants his word plain and passed on. “It hastens to the end” is literally it pants towards the end, like a runner nearing the finish.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith. "Moreover, wine is a traitor, an arrogant man who is never at rest. His greed is as wide as Sheol; like death he has never enough. He gathers for himself all nations and collects as his own all peoples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two lives stand side by side: the proud man, swollen with himself and never satisfied, and the righteous man, who lives by trusting God. This is the verse the whole book turns on.

His soul is puffed up. The first is the proud man, here the Babylonian conqueror: swollen with himself, and “not upright within him”. Everything he has is held by force, and it will not last.

The righteous shall live by his faith. The second is the righteous man, and his whole life is summed up in one phrase. He does not live by explanations, because Habakkuk has not been given many; nor by visible evidence, because the evidence at the moment is an approaching army. He lives by trusting the God who has spoken. So God’s answer to a prophet who cannot understand his times is not a full explanation but an invitation: trust me, and you will live.

Three New Testament quotations. Paul builds on this line his gospel that God justifies sinners through faith in Christ, not by works (Romans 1:17), and quotes it again against those who would add the law to the gospel: “no one is justified before God by the law” (Galatians 3:11). Hebrews uses it to keep struggling Christians from shrinking back (Hebrews 10:38). The New Testament shows where this trust comes to rest: on Christ, in whom God kept his word and through whom he counts the believing sinner righteous (Romans 3:21–26).

The Reformation verse. Martin Luther, agonising over how a sinner could ever be right with God, found the answer through Paul’s use of these words in Romans, and through him the church recovered the truth that God declares sinners righteous through faith alone, not by their works.

Everybody lives by faith. To many modern people faith sounds like a leap in the dark, what you fall back on when the evidence runs out. But Augustine noticed, in his Confessions, how much of his life already rested on trust: in cities he had never visited, in what friends and physicians told him; he could not even know who his parents were except by believing what he had been told. Nobody lives by sight alone. The real question is what we trust, and whether it can bear the weight. Habakkuk sets two lives of faith side by side. The proud man trusts himself, his army and his appetite, the most fragile faith of all. The righteous man trusts the God who has spoken and kept his word. Christian faith is not believing without reasons; it is resting on someone who has given his reasons, above all by keeping his promise in a cross and an empty tomb.

Wine is a traitor. Now the proud man is described further: drunk on success, “never at rest”, his greed “as wide as Sheol”, the grave that never fills. That is greed exactly: it never has enough, and it is the opposite of the quiet life of faith in verse 4.

Where Christians differ: faith or faithfulness? The Hebrew word (emunah) usually means faithfulness, a steadiness that can be relied on, as the ESV footnote notes. So some read the line as saying that the righteous person lives by staying loyal to God, and some think Paul made it say more than it does. This commentary’s view: loyalty to God is true, and Habakkuk shows it in chapter 3, but the steadiness in view here is the steadiness of trust. The contrast is with a man puffed up with self-reliance, and the righteous man is told to hold on to a promise he cannot yet see (vv. 2–3). That is why the Reformed tradition, following the New Testament, reads it as faith. Faith and faithfulness are not rivals: faith leans on God, and faithfulness is that leaning kept up day after day. Neither earns life; both receive it.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament reads my faithfulness: the righteous shall live by God’s faithfulness. Paul leaves the pronoun out (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), and Hebrews attaches it to the righteous person: “my righteous one shall live by faith” (Hebrews 10:38). The readings do not pull against each other. The believer lives by trusting, and what he trusts is the faithfulness of God.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that where the Hebrew text has “wine”, a Dead Sea Scroll reads “wealth”, and that the meaning of these lines is uncertain. Either way the portrait is clear: a man drunk on what he has gained, and never satisfied.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew verse 4b is only three words: “righteous”, “by-his-faith”, “shall-live”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — Woe to the Plunderer and the Builder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whatever is built on plunder and blood is already under God’s woe, because the future belongs to his glory. The nations Babylon has swallowed take up a taunt song. Woe to the one who heaps up what is not his own: his debtors will rise, and the plunderer will be plundered (vv. 6–8). Woe to the one who sets his nest on high with evil gain: the very stones of his house cry out against him (vv. 9–11). Woe to the one who builds a city with blood: the LORD has decreed that such labour only feeds the fire, for the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Wealth and security built on other people collapse, while God's glory is what finally fills the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall not all these take up their taunt against him, with scoffing and riddles for him, and say, "Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own— for how long?— and loads himself with pledges!" Will not your debtors suddenly arise, and those awake who will make you tremble? Then you will be spoil for them. Because you have plundered many nations, all the remnant of the peoples shall plunder you, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations Babylon has robbed will one day rob it: the first woe declares that plunder will be plundered, because God keeps account of blood.

Shall not all these take up their taunt against him? Now come five woes, a mocking song sung by the nations Babylon has swallowed, each stanza beginning the same way. “Woe” echoes the cry of mourning over the dead (1 Kings 13:30), here sung over a man still alive who is as good as dead.

Woe to him who heaps up what is not his own. The first woe is against plunder. “Pledges” is the language of debt: Babylon has taken from everyone, as a ruthless lender takes security from the poor. And the taunt asks Habakkuk’s own question: “for how long?”

Will not your debtors suddenly arise? The debts will be called in. Those who were robbed will rise up, and the plunderer becomes the spoil. Babylon fell to Cyrus and the Medes and Persians in 539 BC, and the wealth of the world changed hands again.

For the blood of man. Under the politics lies a moral principle: “for the blood of man and violence to the earth”. God keeps account of blood. The phrase returns in verse 17, framing the woes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house, to set his nest on high, to be safe from the reach of harm! You have devised shame for your house by cutting off many peoples; you have forfeited your life. For the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beam from the woodwork respond.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second woe falls on the one who builds his own safety out of other people’s ruin, for the very walls of his house will testify against him.

To set his nest on high. The picture is an eagle’s nest, out of reach of predators. That is what the gain is for: safety, a fortified palace, an estate trouble cannot reach.

You have forfeited your life. The house built to protect the family has brought it “shame” instead, and the man who schemed to secure his life has forfeited it. Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns, to whom God said, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20).

The stone will cry out from the wall. The building itself gives evidence: the stone cries out and the beam answers, as one witness answers another in court. Every stone was paid for by somebody, and in God’s court the walls testify.

A modern woe. Much of what people gather is an attempt to build a nest where harm cannot come: enough savings, enough insurance, enough distance from trouble. Providing for a family is good. The mistake is to think such a nest can keep harm out, and the sin is to build it out of someone else’s loss. The only secure height is the one Christ gives, who though he was rich became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who builds a town with blood and founds a city on iniquity! Behold, is it not from the LORD of hosts that peoples labor merely for fire, and nations weary themselves for nothing? For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cities built on bloodshed will burn, because God has decreed that the earth will be filled with his glory, not theirs.

Woe to him who builds a town with blood. The third woe is against public grandeur paid for in human lives. Babylon was famous for its building projects, raised by armies of prisoners and forced labour. Micah said the same of Jerusalem in his day: they “build Zion with blood” (Micah 3:10).

Peoples labor merely for fire. All that work, and it ends as fuel. Not because effort is meaningless in itself, but because the LORD of hosts has decreed that what is built on injustice will burn. The magnificent city became, in time, a mound of ruins in the desert.

As the waters cover the sea. In the middle of five woes, a promise. Empires rise and burn; what finally fills the world is not their glory but God’s, and the filling is total: not puddles here and there, but depth everywhere. Isaiah made the same promise of the reign of the shoot from Jesse (Isaiah 11:9); Habakkuk adds the word “glory”.

Where history is going. Every believer who works at something small and good is working in the same direction as that future, and every empire built on blood is working against it.

When will the earth be filled with the knowledge of his glory? It has begun, as the gospel goes to the nations (Matthew 24:14), for God gives “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). It will be complete when Christ returns and the new creation is lit by God’s glory, with the Lamb as its lamp (Revelation 21:23–26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — Woe to the Degrader and the Idolater
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will turn the degrader’s shame back on him, expose the emptiness of idols, and call the whole earth to silence before him. Woe to the one who makes his neighbour drunk to gaze at his nakedness: the cup in the LORD’s right hand will come round to him, and the violence he did to people and land will overwhelm him (vv. 15–17). An idol is a teacher of lies, trusted by the very man who made it; tell it to wake, and there is no breath in it (vv. 18–19). Against all this noise stands one quiet line: the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who degrade others drink their own cup, and the idols people trust cannot speak; only the living God is to be feared.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink— you pour out your wrath and make them drunk, in order to gaze at their nakedness! You will have your fill of shame instead of glory. Drink, yourself, and show your uncircumcision! The cup in the LORD's right hand will come around to you, and utter shame will come upon your glory! The violence done to Lebanon will overwhelm you, as will the destruction of the beasts that terrified them, for the blood of man and violence to the earth, to cities and all who dwell in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth woe falls on the one who degrades others for his pleasure: the cup of God’s judgment will come round to him, and he will be shamed as he shamed them.

Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink. The picture is of a man who gets his neighbour drunk to humiliate him and enjoy the spectacle. Conquering armies did this literally; Babylon did it to whole nations, stripping them of dignity for the pleasure of watching. The shame of a drunken man’s nakedness is as old as Noah (Genesis 9:21–23).

Drink, yourself. The sentence fits the crime: the cup passes round the table and reaches Babylon at last. “The cup in the LORD’s right hand” is the prophets’ picture of his judgment, which Jeremiah was told to make the nations drink (Jeremiah 25:15–17). “Show your uncircumcision” means: be exposed as one outside God’s covenant, shamed as you shamed others.

The violence done to Lebanon. Babylon stripped the famous cedar forests of Lebanon for its building projects and hunted its wildlife, and God notices that too. The charge repeats the refrain of verse 8, “for the blood of man and violence to the earth”: cruelty to people and destruction of the land are named in one breath.

Christ and the cup. Christians cannot read of this cup without remembering Gethsemane, where Jesus prayed, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and then drank a cup he did not deserve. The only people who will never have to drink it are those for whom he drank it.

In every age. There is a version of this sin in every age: a colleague humiliated for entertainment, someone’s shame exposed online for an audience. God calls it a woe.

Textual note. For “show your uncircumcision” the Dead Sea Scroll commentary on Habakkuk reads “stagger”, and the Greek Old Testament has something similar, which fits the cup of verse 16.

verseByVerse.quote: "What profit is an idol when its maker has shaped it, a metal image, a teacher of lies? For its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols! Woe to him who says to a wooden thing, Awake; to a silent stone, Arise! Can this teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in it. But the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idols are dead things that cannot hear the people who made them and trust them, but the living LORD reigns in his holy temple, and the whole earth must fall silent before him.

What profit is an idol? The fifth woe reaches the root of all the others. The man shaped the thing himself, and now “trusts in his own creation”: in the end he is trusting himself and calling it religion.

A teacher of lies. An idol promises what it cannot give. Modern idols do not usually have faces; they are the career, the family name, the political cause, the pension. What they share with the ancient kind is that we made them, and they cannot save us. “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8).

There is no breath at all in it. Picture the scene: a man in front of a carved block, shouting “Awake”, and nothing happens. The gold plating is beautiful, and the thing is dead.

But the LORD is in his holy temple. After the roaring of armies, the boasting of the proud and the shouting at wooden gods, a sentence of extraordinary calm. He has not left his throne; he is not asleep, absent or unaware.

Let all the earth keep silence before him. The right response is not more noise but silence, the hush of a courtroom when the judge enters (compare Zephaniah 1:7; Zechariah 2:13).

The true image. The idol is an image with no breath in it. The living God forbade such images, and then gave one of his own: his Son, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), who speaks, hears and saves.

The turning point. Habakkuk began the book shouting questions at heaven, and he will end it singing. This verse is the turning point, and it is where every believer who has been arguing with God must come to stand: not with all the answers, but quiet before the God who has them.

2.title: The Righteous Shall Live by His Faith
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with Habakkuk asking whether the conqueror would go on emptying his net forever. Now he climbs his watchpost, and God answers with the book’s most famous line (v. 4) and his verdict on Babylon.

The message. God’s word will be fulfilled at his appointed time, however slow it seems, so wait for it. Meanwhile two lives stand side by side: the proud, who trust themselves and are never satisfied, and the righteous, who live by trusting God. Every power built on plunder, blood and idols is already under God’s woe, and history ends not in its glory but in his, filling the earth.

Why it was said. The faithful in Judah faced a Babylonian invasion God himself had announced (1:5–11; see the introduction). They needed to know whether evil would have the last word, and how to live meanwhile.

How the chapter makes its case. The prophet takes his stand to wait, and God tells him to write the vision plainly, for it has an appointed time and will surely come (vv. 1–3). Then the contrast that sums up the book: the puffed-up man, as greedy as the grave, and the righteous who shall live by his faith (vv. 4–5). The plundered nations sing five woes: on plunder, which will be plundered (vv. 6–8); on a nest set high with evil gain (vv. 9–11); on a city built with blood, for the earth will be filled with the LORD’s glory, not its own (vv. 12–14); on degrading one’s neighbours, for the LORD’s cup will come round (vv. 15–17); and on breathless idols (vv. 18–19). Last comes a hush: the LORD is in his holy temple (v. 20).

Where it leads. To Christ above all by promise. Hebrews reads the vision that “will surely come” as the return of Christ (Hebrews 10:37), and Paul makes verse 4 the banner of the gospel, “The righteous shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11): righteous not by works but by trusting the God who justifies sinners in Christ. The cup in the LORD’s right hand (v. 16) is the cup Jesus asked might pass from him and then drank (Matthew 26:39), so that it need never reach those who trust him. And the earth filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory (v. 14) is the world where “the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

For us. When God seems slow, wait for him: his promises keep their appointed time. Live by faith, not by sight, and not by the self-reliance that puffs the soul up. Build nothing on another’s loss, trust nothing your hands have made, and be still before the God who is in his holy temple.
2.theology:
Honest prayer waits for God's answer and is willing to be corrected by it (v. 1).

God gives his answers in writing, so that they can be read, remembered and passed on (v. 2).

God's promises have an appointed time; what looks slow to us is exactly on time from where God stands (v. 3; Heb 10:37).

The righteous live by faith in God rather than by explanations or visible evidence; this is the verse on which Paul builds justification by faith (v. 4; Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38).

Greed is an appetite that can never be filled, the opposite of the quiet life of faith (v. 5).

Wealth, security and grandeur built on other people are repaid in kind, and the very stones bear witness (vv. 6-13).

The earth's future is not the glory of empires but the knowledge of God's glory filling it completely (v. 14; Isa 11:9).

Idols are lies we make and then trust, and the God who is in his holy temple silences every rival (vv. 18-20).
2.examples:
The chapter begins with a prophet climbing his tower to wait for a reply, and a message written large enough to read at a run. At its heart stand two men side by side, one swollen with himself and with an appetite as wide as the grave, the other living by trust.

The woes give their own pictures: an eagle's nest built high with other people's money, stones in a wall giving evidence in court, and a man shouting “Awake!” at a block of gold-plated wood, while the living God sits unhurried in his holy temple.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, his soul is puffed up; it is not upright within him, but the righteous shall live by his faith.
keyVerse.note: God’s answer to a prophet who cannot understand his times is not a full explanation but a way to live. The proud man trusts himself and will fall; the righteous man trusts God and will live. Quoted three times in the New Testament, this line became the banner of the gospel and of the Reformation: we are counted righteous not by what we do but by trusting the God who justifies sinners through Christ.

2.reflection:
Habakkuk takes his stand to wait, ready to be corrected by God’s answer (v. 1). How do you wait when prayer seems unanswered? Are you as ready for God’s answer to correct you as to comfort you?

“If it seems slow, wait for it; it will surely come” (v. 3). Which of God’s promises do you find hardest to wait for, and how does Hebrews 10:37, which applies this verse to Christ’s return, help?

Verse 4 sets the proud man beside the righteous man who lives by faith. What does living by faith rather than by self-reliance look like in an ordinary week? How does Paul’s use of the verse (Romans 1:17) deepen what faith means?

The five woes condemn plunder, security built on others’ loss, grandeur built on blood, degrading others, and idols (vv. 6–19). Which of these has a modern form in our world or in our own hearts? How does the promise of verse 14 change the way you see your own work?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s work frightens us, faith asks for mercy and remembers how he came before. Habakkuk’s prayer, set to music, begins in awe at what God has said he will do, and asks three things: revive your work in our days, make it known, and in wrath remember mercy (vv. 1–2). Then he recalls God coming from Teman and Paran, the desert of Sinai, his splendour covering the heavens, light flashing from his hand, plague and pestilence attending him like servants (vv. 3–5). He stands, and the nations shake and the everlasting hills sink low; only his ways are everlasting, and the desert peoples tremble in their tents (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The right prayer in a dark time is that God would act again as he has acted before, and remember mercy in the middle of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth. O LORD, I have heard the report of you, and your work, O LORD, do I fear. In the midst of the years revive it; in the midst of the years make it known; in wrath remember mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frightened by what God has said he will do, Habakkuk prays that God would act again in his own day, and in the middle of judgment remember mercy.

A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet. The book ends as a psalm. Shigionoth is a musical direction, like “Selah” (three times in this chapter) and the note at the end of verse 19: this prayer was meant to be sung in public worship. A man’s private wrestling with God became a song for the congregation, which is why so many believers in trouble find their own words in Scripture.

Your work, O LORD, do I fear. Habakkuk has heard what God is going to do, and it frightens him. He does not pretend to be braver than he is.

In the midst of the years revive it. Three short petitions worth learning by heart. “Revive it”: do again, in our own time, what you have done before. “Make it known”: let people see it. And the loveliest: “in wrath remember mercy”.

In wrath remember mercy. He does not ask God to cancel the judgment; he has accepted that it is just. He asks that in the middle of it God would not forget to be merciful, for he had shown himself to Moses as “merciful and gracious, slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6). It is a prayer for a nation under discipline, a church in decline, a family reaping what it has sown.

Wrath and mercy met. God answered this prayer most fully at the cross. There his wrath against sin was not cancelled but borne, and his mercy reached sinners through it (Romans 3:25–26).

Uncertain wording. Shigionoth occurs only here. A related word heads Psalm 7 (Shiggaion), and some think both mean an impassioned, irregular kind of song, perhaps a lament; the exact meaning is unknown. Selah probably marks a pause or interlude.
verseByVerse.note: The title of Psalm 7 uses a related word, Shiggaion; some think both mean an impassioned, irregular kind of song.

verseByVerse.quote: God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. His brightness was like the light; rays flashed from his hand; and there he veiled his power. Before him went pestilence, and plague followed at his heels. He stood and measured the earth; he looked and shook the nations; then the eternal mountains were scattered; the everlasting hills sank low. His were the everlasting ways. I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction; the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Habakkuk remembers God coming to his people at Sinai in overwhelming glory, when nations and ancient mountains shook before him, because the God who came then can be trusted to come again.

God came from Teman, and the Holy One from Mount Paran. Now the prayer becomes a vision of the past. Teman and Paran lie in the desert country to the south, the region of Sinai, and Moses used the same geography in his blessing: “he shone forth from Mount Paran” (Deuteronomy 33:2; compare Judges 5:4–5).

Remembering in the dark. Unable to see God at work in his own day, he remembers what God has already done.

There he veiled his power. A striking line: even this blaze of light is God holding his power back. What people can bear to see is only the edge of his glory.

Before him went pestilence. Plague and pestilence walk before him and at his heels, like servants attending a king, recalling the plagues of Egypt. Even the forces that terrify us are on a lead in his hand.

He stood and measured the earth. He has only to stand and look, and the nations shake. The eternal mountains and everlasting hills turn out not to be everlasting at all: “His were the everlasting ways”. Only God is permanent.

The tents of Cushan. Desert peoples on the route of the exodus shake in their tents as God passes. The point is not their guilt but the sheer effect of his approach.

Glory veiled. The glory that blazed from Paran veiled itself more deeply still in Christ, hidden in an ordinary man so that sinners could come near and live: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14).

Uncertain wording. “Rays flashed from his hand” renders a word that usually means horns; here it means beams of light, from the same root as the verb used when the skin of Moses’ face “shone” (Exodus 34:29). Cushan occurs only here; set beside Midian, it probably names a desert people near Midian rather than Cush (Ethiopia).
verseByVerse.note: Teman was a district of Edom, and Paran the wilderness between Sinai and Canaan.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All God’s power in the exodus was spent for one purpose: to save his people. Was the LORD angry with the rivers and the sea? No: he was riding his chariot of salvation (v. 8). He drew his bow and split the earth with rivers; the mountains writhed, the deep cried out, and sun and moon stood still at the flash of his arrows (vv. 9–11). He marched through the earth in fury for one reason, the salvation of his people and his anointed. He crushed the head of the house of the wicked, turned the enemy’s own weapons against him, and trampled the sea with his horses (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's terrifying power in history is aimed at one thing: the rescue of his people through his anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: Was your wrath against the rivers, O LORD? Was your anger against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you rode on your horses, on your chariot of salvation? You stripped the sheath from your bow, calling for many arrows. Selah You split the earth with rivers. The mountains saw you and writhed; the raging waters swept on; the deep gave forth its voice; it lifted its hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of your arrows as they sped, at the flash of your glittering spear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s overwhelming power over sea and river, sun and moon, was never temper against creation: it was spent on one purpose, the rescue of his people.

Was your wrath against the rivers, O LORD? When God split the sea at the exodus and stopped the Jordan, was he angry with the water? Of course not. He was riding “on your chariot of salvation”: the whole display of power had one purpose, to rescue his people.

You stripped the sheath from your bow. God bares his bow like a warrior going into battle, and splits the earth with rivers, perhaps recalling the water he brought from the rock in the desert.

The mountains saw you and writhed. Creation responds like a living thing: the mountains writhe, and the deep cries out and lifts its hands like a man surrendering. Even “the sun and moon stood still”, as in Joshua’s day (Joshua 10:12–13), outshone by the light of God’s arrows.

Who then is this? The God who rode upon the sea stood one night in a fishing boat on Galilee and rebuked the wind and the waves, and his frightened disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41).

When God shakes things. When God shakes things in our lives, it is not a burst of temper. He is going somewhere, and the destination is salvation.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of “calling for many arrows” (v. 9) is uncertain, and translations vary widely. Whatever the details, the picture is of God armed and going out to battle.

verseByVerse.quote: You marched through the earth in fury; you threshed the nations in anger. You went out for the salvation of your people, for the salvation of your anointed. You crushed the head of the house of the wicked, laying him bare from thigh to neck. Selah You pierced with his own arrows the heads of his warriors, who came like a whirlwind to scatter me, rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret. You trampled the sea with your horses, the surging of mighty waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God marched through the nations for the salvation of his people and his anointed king, and struck their enemy a crushing blow to the head.

You went out for the salvation of your people. The centre of the vision, where one word comes twice: salvation. God’s marching and threshing are not random violence; he goes out to save.

For the salvation of your anointed. First, the king God had chosen to lead his people, and through him the people. Christians cannot help reading further. The Hebrew word for anointed is the word from which we get “Messiah”, and the Bible’s story runs toward one Anointed through whom God saves.

You crushed the head of the house of the wicked. The enemy falls by a blow to the head. Ever since Eden God’s promise has been that the offspring of the woman would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). Many Christians hear in this rescue an echo of that promise, which was kept at the cross, where Christ destroyed “the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14).

You pierced with his own arrows. The enemy is destroyed with his own weapons. The men who came “rejoicing as if to devour the poor in secret” discover that the poor have a defender.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in the rest of verse 13, “laying him bare from thigh to neck”, is uncertain; it reads literally foundation to neck. It seems to picture a house, or a man, stripped from bottom to top: total overthrow.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Though the Fig Tree Should Not Blossom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith can rejoice in God when everything else has gone. The prophet shakes from head to foot at what is coming, yet resolves to wait quietly for the day when God will deal with the invader (v. 16). Then he imagines the worst, every crop and every animal gone (v. 17), and answers it with one word, “yet”: he will rejoice in the LORD, the God of his salvation, who is his strength and makes his feet as sure as a deer’s on the heights (vv. 18–19). The complaint of chapter 1 has become a song for the choir.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith's final word is joy in God himself, which survives when every visible support is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: I hear, and my body trembles; my lips quiver at the sound; rottenness enters into my bones; my legs tremble beneath me. Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us. Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shaking with dread at the coming invasion, Habakkuk still resolves to wait quietly for God’s judgment, and he faces honestly the loss of everything that keeps his people alive.

My body trembles. Habakkuk’s calm is not numbness. Read the symptoms: trembling body, quivering lips, rottenness in his bones, shaking legs. He is physically shaking with dread at the invasion he knows is coming.

Yet I will quietly wait. In that state he says “yet”. Faith is not the absence of fear; it is trusting God while afraid. And he knows what he is waiting for: “the day of trouble” for the invaders, the judgment on Babylon announced in the woes (2:6–20). This is the waiting God asked of him at the watchpost: “If it seems slow, wait for it” (2:3).

Though the fig tree should not blossom. A sentence built like a staircase going down. Count what is removed: blossom on the fig tree, fruit on the vines, olives, food from the fields, sheep in the fold, cattle in the stalls. For a farming people these six clauses are not poetry but starvation: fig, vine and olive were the staple crops, flocks and herds the savings account. It is exactly what an invading army leaves behind.

Facing the worst. He does not pretend the fig tree will blossom after all. He faces the worst honestly, and then speaks the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation. GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer's; he makes me tread on my high places. To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing left but God, Habakkuk rejoices in him, and finds that the God of his salvation gives him strength and sure feet on the heights.

Yet I will rejoice in the LORD. Everything hangs on that word “yet”. The barns are empty, and the sentence turns. Look where the joy is: in the LORD, in “the God of my salvation”. Not in the harvest, not in a better season next year, not even in Babylon’s promised fall. His joy has moved from God’s gifts to God himself, the one joy no invading army can take.

The answer to chapter 1. Habakkuk never gets a full explanation of why God uses wicked nations, and neither will we for much of what we go through. What he gets is God, and it turns out to be enough.

He makes my feet like the deer’s. The final picture is a deer on a mountainside, running surefooted along ledges where a man would fall. God does not remove the heights; he gives sure feet to walk on them. David sang the same: “He made my feet like the feet of a deer” (Psalm 18:33).

To the choirmaster. The book that began with “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help” ends with a note for the worship leader, “with stringed instruments” (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads “my stringed”). The complaint has become a hymn.

What his salvation cost. Christians can say this “yet” with more reason still. The God of our salvation has shown what it cost him: he did not spare his own Son, and Paul argues from that gift that he will not withhold anything we truly need (Romans 8:32). Peter wrote to believers who had lost a great deal that their inheritance is “kept in heaven for you”, beyond the reach of decay, and that they rejoice in Christ even while grieved by trials (1 Peter 1:4–8). The fig tree may fail. Christ will not.

Learned contentment. Paul learned the same lesson: “I have learned, in whatever situation I am, to be content”, in “plenty and hunger, abundance and need” (Philippians 4:11–12). Contentment is not a temperament but a discipline, and this chapter shows how it is learned: remember what God has done, look honestly at what may come, and find your joy in God himself, where loss cannot reach it.

When you cannot yet say it. If you are in the middle of loss and cannot yet say “yet”, remember that Habakkuk reached it by way of quivering lips and shaking legs (v. 16). Joy in God is not a mood you must produce before he will help you. He grows it, often slowly, in people who keep bringing him their grief.

The journey of the book. Bring God your hardest questions; wait for his answer; learn that the righteous live by faith; and find, when everything that can be shaken is shaken, that joy in God himself is still standing.

3.title: Yet I Will Rejoice in the LORD
3.overview:
Where we are. God has answered Habakkuk in chapter 2: the vision will surely come, the righteous live by faith, and Babylon is under his woe. Now the prophet who began with a complaint ends with a prayer set to music.

The message. When the future looks dark, faith remembers what God has done and trusts him for what he will do. The God who came down at the exodus to save his people will come again for their salvation, so even if everything else is taken from them, they can rejoice in him. Habakkuk’s questions are not all answered, but the questioner has been changed.

Why it was said. Judah faced invasion, famine and exile (see the introduction), and the faithful needed a song for the waiting.

How the chapter makes its case. The prayer opens with fear and a plea: revive your work in our days, and in wrath remember mercy (vv. 1–2). Then the prophet remembers God coming from the south as at Sinai, while the ancient mountains sank before him (vv. 3–7). Was God angry with the rivers and the sea? No: he was riding his chariot of salvation (vv. 8–11). He marched through the earth for the salvation of his people and his anointed, and crushed the head of the wicked (vv. 12–15). The prophet trembles, yet resolves to wait quietly for the day of trouble to fall on the invader (v. 16); and though fig, vine, olive, field, flock and herd should all fail, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation, who makes his feet like the deer’s (vv. 17–19).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. The exodus Habakkuk remembers is the pattern of every rescue God would work, and Jesus spoke of his own “departure”, in Greek his exodus, to be accomplished at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). God goes out “for the salvation of your anointed” (v. 13), the word from which “Messiah” comes, and crushes the head of the wicked, echoing the promise that the serpent’s head would be crushed (Genesis 3:15), kept when Christ by his death destroyed “the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). And the prayer “in wrath remember mercy” (v. 2) was answered most fully at the cross, where God’s wrath against sin and his mercy to sinners met in one person.

For us. Christians can say Habakkuk’s “yet” with more reason than he could, for the God of our salvation did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32). When you cannot see what God is doing, remember what he has done; tremble honestly if you must, but wait; and seek your joy in God himself, where no loss can reach it.
3.theology:
Honest wrestling with God can become public worship; Scripture takes lament into worship by setting it to music (v. 1).

The right prayer under judgment is that God would act again as he has acted before, and remember mercy in the midst of wrath (v. 2).

Remembering what God has done is the believer's resource when he cannot see what God is doing (vv. 3-7).

God's displays of power are not temper but purpose: he rides a chariot of salvation (v. 8).

God acts in history for the rescue of his people through his anointed, crushing the head of the enemy as promised in Eden (v. 13; Gen 3:15).

Faith is not the absence of fear but trust in God while trembling (v. 16).

Joy that rests on God himself, rather than on his gifts, survives the loss of everything (vv. 17-18; Phil 4:11-13).

God does not remove the heights but gives sure feet to walk on them (v. 19; Ps 18:33).
3.examples:
In this chapter a private argument with God becomes a hymn for the congregation, and a prayer asks for mercy inside the judgment, not instead of it. even God’s blazing light is said to veil his power; the everlasting hills turn out not to be everlasting; the sea is split open, not because God was angry with water but because he was riding to save.

And at the end a believer shaking from head to foot counts six empty things and says “yet”, and runs like a deer along a ledge where a man would fall.

keyVerse.quote: Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls, yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.
keyVerse.note: These verses are where the whole book arrives. The prophet who began by asking “how long?” now imagines losing everything that keeps his people alive, and answers it with one word, “yet”. His joy has moved from God’s gifts to God himself, and so nothing an army can take away can take it. In Christ, believers have even more reason to sing it, for the God of their salvation gave his own Son for them.

3.reflection:
Habakkuk prays, “in wrath remember mercy” (v. 2). Where would you pray that prayer today, for yourself, your family, your church or your country? How does the cross give us confidence to pray it?

In the dark, Habakkuk remembers what God did at the exodus (vv. 3–15). What has God done, in Scripture and in your own life, that you can remember when you cannot see what he is doing now?

Habakkuk’s body shakes, and yet he resolves to wait (v. 16). How does his honesty about fear help someone who thinks that faith means always feeling calm?

What are the “fig trees” you most depend on (v. 17)? What would it mean to rejoice in God himself if they failed, and how does Romans 8:32 make that more than wishful thinking?
